documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                )                     Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                        CORPORATE ENERGY BUYERS ASSOCIATION


           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC

or Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Corporate Energy Buyers Association

(CEBA) respectfully submits this motion for leave to answer and limited answer to the answer

filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) in this proceeding. 2 CEBA submits this answer to

correct PJM’s characterization of CEBA’s position regarding customer-sponsored Peak Shaving

Adjustments and to explain why the PJM Answer does not resolve the undue preference

identified in CEBA’s protest. 3


I.         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

           Although Rule 213(a)(2) does not generally permit answers to protests, the Commission

permits answers for good cause shown, such as when an answer contributes to a more accurate

and complete record or provides useful information that aids the Commission’s decision-making

process. 4 CEBA respectfully moves for leave to file this answer because it responds to



1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
    PJM Sept. 23 Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer (PJM Answer).
3
    CEBA Sept. 3 Motion to Intervene and Protest (CEBA Protest).
4
 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,110, at P 22 (2024) (accepting answers to protests and
answers because they assisted the Commission in its decision-making process).
 arguments raised in the PJM Answer that mischaracterize CEBA’s position. As discussed below,

PJM’s arguments do not address an issue that the Commission must help resolve in order to

ensure that large load customers can invest with confidence in a full range of solutions to the

resource adequacy challenges confronting the PJM region. For this reason, good cause exists for

the Commission to grant this motion.


II.      ANSWER

         The PJM Answer does not resolve the disparate treatment identified in CEBA’s Protest.

Instead, PJM responds to an argument CEBA did not make. PJM characterizes CEBA and other

intervenors as challenging the “omission of Peak Shaving Adjustment MW from [Bring Your

Own New Capacity (BYONC)] arrangements” and ultimately concludes that Peak Shaving

Adjustments (PSAs) “cannot and should not qualify as BYONC MW capable of reducing

[Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS)] exposure.” 5 But CEBA did not ask PJM to treat

PSA MW as BYONC, permit them to participate as Capacity Resources in capacity auctions

(Reliability Pricing Model [RPM] Auctions), or make them dispatchable during an IRAS Action.

CEBA asked for a tariff-based mechanism that recognizes incremental, customer-sponsored

PSAs that reduce PJM’s capacity requirement, including qualifying investments elsewhere

within the relevant utility service territory or zone. 6


5
  PJM Answer at 47–48, n.170 (characterizing CEBA and other intervenors as challenging the “omission of Peak
Shaving Adjustment MW from BYONC arrangements” and concluding that Peak Shaving Adjustments “cannot and
should not qualify as BYONC MW capable of reducing IRAS exposure”).
6
  CEBA Protest at 8–9 (requesting “a clear tariff-based mechanism” for recognition of “incremental, customer-
sponsored Peak Shaving Adjustments that reduce PJM’s capacity requirement,” including qualifying investments
elsewhere within the relevant utility service territory or zone, and explaining that the requested treatment would
permit New Large Loads to address resource adequacy through “either incremental supply or an incremental
reduction in the capacity requirement”).




                                                          2
            Fundamentally, CEBA seeks recognition of incremental, customer-sponsored PSAs for

what they are: reductions in forecast peak demand that reduce the underlying capacity need

associated with new load growth. The IRAS proposal is patently unjust, unreasonable, and

unduly preferential insofar as it fails to recognize that core resource adequacy benefit of

customer-sponsored PSAs.

           A.       PJM conflates reducing the capacity need with providing a Capacity

                    Resource while failing to reconcile its position with its treatment of PSAs

                    under the RBP proposal

           PJM conflates two distinct ways of addressing a resource adequacy need: adding capacity

to meet incremental demand and reducing the incremental demand for which capacity must be

procured. PJM emphasizes that PSA MW are “adjustments to PJM’s load forecasts, not

resources that may participate in RPM Auctions.” 7 That distinction does not rebut CEBA’s

argument; it is the premise of it. As CEBA has previously argued, PJM’s own rules recognize

qualifying PSAs as reductions to forecast peak demand and, therefore, to the capacity

requirement that PJM must satisfy when procuring capacity, whether through the RBP or RPM

Auctions. 8 The fact that the reduction occurs on the demand side rather than through the addition




7
    PJM Answer at 47.
8
    CEBA Protest at 8, n.13 (citing PJM Manual 19, Load Forecasting and Analysis, § 3.2).




                                                          3
 of a Capacity Resource does not eliminate that resource adequacy benefit, nor does PJM offer

evidence to the contrary. 9

            PJM’s discussion of the RBP reinforces this point. PJM notes that qualifying PSA MW

may reduce the identified capacity shortfall for which the RBP will procure while PSA MW

cannot serve as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW or eligible RBP Resources. CEBA does not

contend otherwise. The relevant feature of the RBP is that PJM recognizes qualifying PSAs on

the demand side of the equation by reducing the capacity shortfall—quantified in the RBP Initial

Procurement Target—that must be addressed through new supply. CEBA seeks comparable

recognition here: not treatment of PSA MW as supply, but recognition that incremental,

customer-sponsored peak shaving reduces the capacity need attributable to the sponsoring New

Large Load.

            B.     PJM’s reliance on real-time dispatchability misses the point

            PJM’s observation that PSA MW are not “real-time dispatchable” is irrelevant. 10 As PJM

itself explains, “[t]he impetus for IRAS is to incent New Large Loads to bring new capacity to

meet their resource adequacy needs.” 11 If an incremental, qualifying PSA reduces PJM’s

forecast peak in the first instance and therefore reduces the amount of capacity that must be

procured to meet a New Large Load’s resource adequacy needs, that capacity need has been

reduced before any real-time IRAS Action ever occurs. PJM does not explain why real-time


9
 Moreover, in the IRAS proposal, PJM itself recognizes that a Peak Shaving Adjustment may “reduce the amount of
capacity needed to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement.” PJM Filing, Transmittal at 54.
10
  PJM Answer at 48 (explaining that Peak Shaving Adjustments are not a “real-time dispatchable product” and
therefore, in PJM’s view, should not qualify as BYONC MW capable of reducing IRAS exposure).
11
     Id. at 45.




                                                       4
 dispatchability is necessary to recognize that reduction when determining the amount of a New

Large Load’s demand that gives rise to IRAS exposure in the first place. 12

            C.     PJM’s disparate treatment of customer-sponsored PSAs is unjustified and

                   counterproductive to state-led efforts to support resource adequacy

            Under the IRAS proposal, the disparate treatment is straightforward. Consider two

otherwise identical New Large Loads. One customer supports new Capacity Resources that PJM

determines provide 25 MW of capacity toward addressing the incremental resource adequacy

need associated with its load. The other finances qualifying incremental peak-shaving capability

that reduces PJM’s forecast peak demand and, after application of the Forecast Pool

Requirement, reduces PJM’s capacity requirement by the same 25 MW. PJM’s proposal

recognizes the first customer’s contribution in determining its IRAS exposure but provides no

comparable mechanism to recognize the second. PJM identifies differences between Capacity

Resources and PSAs, but it does not explain why those differences justify treating differently

two investments that reduce PJM’s otherwise-unmet capacity need by the same amount.

            In addressing other parties’ tangential arguments about BYONC gating criteria for

Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources—both supply-side Capacity

Resources—PJM implies that its skepticism toward customer-sponsored PSAs may similarly

stem from concern that such investments will not produce “new and lasting” solutions to the

capacity shortfall. 13 Customer-sponsored PSAs can rely on the same types of distributed energy



12
     Id. at 48.
13
  Id. at 49 (“IRAS is an operational tool designed to address the shortfall created by the absence of new Capacity
Resources that offer lasting solutions to the capacity shortfall.”).




                                                          5
 infrastructure, including distributed battery storage, that support aggregations participating as

supply-side Capacity Resources. Yet PJM has established BYONC gating criteria to ensure that

Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources provide “new and lasting capacity

contributions to the capacity shortfall.” 14 Although the criteria may differ, CEBA asks only that

customer-sponsored PSAs have a similar opportunity to demonstrate that their underlying

infrastructure investments can provide lasting resource adequacy benefits.

        Lastly, PJM’s disparate treatment between customer-sponsored PSAs and Capacity

Resources could foreclose a valuable source of investment in precisely the types of near-term,

distributed-scale solutions that states are actively seeking to develop, particularly in the face of

persistent barriers to interconnecting new, utility-scale generation. Virginia and New Jersey, for

example, are pursuing programs to deploy distributed battery storage and other distributed

resources to reduce peak demand and associated capacity needs. 15 A framework that recognizes

customer investment in new Capacity Resources but provides no means to recognize customer

investment in qualifying Peak Shaving Adjustments would eliminate an important incentive for

New Large Loads to help finance these emerging pathways and frustrate legitimate state policy

goals aiming to unlock these innovative approaches.




14
  Id. at 48–49 (explaining the purpose of PJM’s requirement for BYONC that is backed by Demand Resources and
DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to demonstrate Accredited UCAP each year of the 10-year BYONC
commitment period).
15
  Chief Energy Officer for the Governor of Virginia Sept. 3 Comments at 2–3 (“Virginia has already acted to
establish pathways for voluntary demand-flexibility programs that enable large loads to secure measurable and
verifiable load reductions…. PJM’s rules should provide a clear, timely, and administrable process through which
these state-supported arrangements can be recognized in IRAS…, with such reductions accounted for in a
customer’s curtailment exposure and related obligations.”); see also New Jersey Board of Public Utilities Sept. 18
Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer at 4–5.




                                                         6
            D.       Customer-sponsored PSAs and new Capacity Resources are complementary

                    pieces to the resource adequacy puzzle


           To reiterate, CEBA is not asking the Commission to transform PSAs into Capacity

Resources or to require PJM to count PSA MW as BYONC. Rather, PJM should revise proposed

Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V(b), to recognize the reduction in PJM’s capacity requirement

attributable to a verified, incremental, customer-sponsored PSA when determining the

sponsoring New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount. 16 PJM should apply the

Forecast Pool Requirement as needed to express that benefit in the units used by section V(b),

and establish appropriate rules for verification and safeguard against double counting. This

would recognize the PSA’s effect on resource adequacy without treating it as BYONC or as a

resource PJM can dispatch during an IRAS Action.


           This approach preserves the distinction on which PJM relies. BYONC supplies

incremental capacity; PSAs reduce forecast demand. But both can support resource adequacy by

reducing the incremental capacity need associated with a New Large Load. PJM has not

explained why IRAS should recognize only one side of that equation.


III.       CONCLUSION


           For the foregoing reasons, CEBA respectfully asks that the Commission accept this

answer in the record and find that PJM’s IRAS proposal is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly

preferential insofar as it provides no mechanism to recognize the reduction in PJM’s capacity


16
     PJM Filing, Attach. A, Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, § V(b).




                                                           7
 requirement attributable to a verified, incremental, customer-sponsored PSA when determining

the sponsoring New Large Load’s IRAS exposure. CEBA asks the Commission to require PJM

to provide such a mechanism, with appropriate verification, attribution, and safeguards against

double counting.




Respectfully submitted,
